claims.text: The as-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a high caloric effect.
The as-cast alloy has poor mechanical integrity and forms cracks under cyclic loading.
A thin high-modulus metallic coating will reduce surface-crack initiation and propagation in the target alloy.
Reducing surface cracking with the coating will significantly improve the mechanical integrity of the target alloy.
The coating will preserve the alloy's large caloric response during applied-field and pressure-field operation.
The proposed intervention is a 2–5 μm Cr or Cr–Mo coating sputtered at a substrate temperature of 300–400 °C.
An optimized interlayer will enhance coating adhesion.
A low-temperature post-deposition anneal will promote compressive residual stress and robust interfacial bonding.
Sputtering can produce a continuous, dense, fine-structured metallic film with a uniform thickness and substantial film stress.
The proposed coating on the target alloy will be adherent and possess intrinsic compressive residual stress.
A surface film or interface can act as a barrier that hinders crack propagation.
Coating-induced surface compression will impede crack nucleation and propagation.
Limiting the coating thickness to 2–5 μm will leave the bulk transformation characteristics responsible for the caloric response unaltered.
The coating will produce a notable reduction in surface-crack density.
The coated alloy will have approximately 20–50% greater tensile or compressive strength than the uncoated alloy.
The coated alloy's caloric performance will remain within ±10% of the uncoated baseline.
The improvement will persist under applied magnetic fields, pressure fields, moderate thermal cycling, and cyclic mechanical loading typical of caloric applications.
Long-term coating adhesion and thermal stability under repeated mechanical and thermal cycling are uncertain.
